# Week 1: Introduction to R Programming {#sec-week1}

```{r}
#| include: false
set.seed(7432)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center")
```

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (6, 4)
```

Welcome to MATH7432! Over the next five weeks we will learn how to program — in R or in
Python, your choice — and how to use it to build the computational tools that modern
statistics runs on. By the end of the module you will have implemented, from scratch,
algorithms that estimate statistical models — the same family of algorithms that trains
neural networks. This week we start from zero: no programming background is assumed.

Before the code, three definitions, compressed as much as academically acceptable.
A **computer** is a device with a processor (which does arithmetic, very fast), memory (which
holds the numbers the processor is currently working on) and storage (which holds files that
survive a reboot). A **program** is a list of instructions for the processor. Processors only
understand *machine code* — streams of 0s and 1s — which humans are famously bad at writing,
so we write programs in a **programming language**: a formal language that is readable by
humans and translated for the machine. R and Python — the two languages of this module — are
both *high-level*, *interpreted* languages: high-level means they read almost like
mathematics, and interpreted means each line is translated and executed on the spot, so you
can have a live conversation with your computer — type a command, get an answer, type the
next one. This makes them ideal for data analysis, where you rarely know step 10 before
seeing the result of step 3.

**R** was created in 1993 by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman in Auckland as an open-source
descendant of the S language, and it has since become the lingua franca of statistics: free,
open source, with thousands of contributed packages covering essentially every statistical
method ever published.

**Python** was created in 1991 by Guido van Rossum in the Netherlands, and is named after
the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake. It is a free, open-source, general-purpose
language with a philosophy of readability, and — through the libraries numpy and pandas,
which we will lean on heavily — it has become the other lingua franca of scientific
computing, and the language most machine learning is written in.

A good statistician picks the right tool for the task, and today the tasks of statistics
are done in these two. In this module you are expected to *learn one of them* — your pick,
unless your programme has already picked for you. Every example in these notes appears in
both languages, so whichever you choose, the notes double as a dictionary for reading the
other.

If you have ever felt that working with data means being trapped in a spreadsheet, dragging
formulas across cells until the heat death of the universe:

![](images/chapter1/skyrim-finally-awake.jpg){width="450" fig-alt="Skyrim meme: 'Hey you, you're finally awake.'"}

Throughout these notes you will meet chunks of code with their output printed underneath —
**side by side in the two languages, R always on the left, Python always on the right** (on
a narrow screen the columns stack, and the bold label above each chunk tells you which is
which). Follow the column of the language you are learning; glancing at the other one
occasionally is how you become bilingual for free:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
# I am a comment: R ignores everything after a '#'. The line below does the work.
print("Beep bop beep")
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
# I am a comment: Python ignores everything after a '#'. The line below does the work.
print("Beep bop beep")
```

</div>
:::

The notes are designed for the labs: read a section, copy the code into RStudio, run it,
break it, fix it, and do the exercises as you meet them. Programming is not a spectator
sport.

## R and RStudio

You will interact with R through **RStudio**, a program that wraps R in a friendly interface.
Both are installed on the university machines; for your own laptop, install R from
[r-project.org](https://www.r-project.org) first and RStudio from
[posit.co](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) second. When you open RStudio you will
see several panels:

-   the **console** (look for the `>` prompt): type a command, press `Enter`, R answers
    immediately;
-   the **script editor**: a text file of commands you are preparing. Press `Ctrl + Enter`
    (`Cmd + Enter` on a Mac) on a line to send it to the console;
-   the **environment** panel: lists the objects you have created so far;
-   a miscellaneous panel showing files, plots and help pages.

**Note for Python users:** everything in this section applies to you too. RStudio speaks
Python as well, and it is what we use in the labs for both languages: a Python script ends
in `.py` instead of `.R`, the Python console prompt is `>>>` rather than `>`, and on your
own laptop you will want Python from [python.org](https://www.python.org) (the university
machines have it already). Comments are `#` in Python too, so everything below about
commenting transfers unchanged.

The console is for experiments; a **script** (a plain text file with extension `.R`, created
via *File > New File > R Script*) is for anything you want to keep. The console forgets, a
saved script does not. A good workflow, and the one to use in the labs, is: type your commands
in a script, run them with `Ctrl + Enter`, and save the script as you go. Future you, who
returns after a week and remembers nothing, will be grateful.

Future you will be even more grateful for **comments**. Any text after a `#` on a line is
ignored, in both languages, which makes it the place to explain *why* the code does what it
does:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
# convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit
20 * 9 / 5 + 32
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
# convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit
20 * 9 / 5 + 32
```

</div>
:::

We comment code generously in these notes, and you should do the same in yours.

### Getting help

Every R function has a help page: `?seq` (or `help(seq)`) opens the documentation for `seq`.
The *Description*, *Usage* and *Arguments* sections are the ones to read first, and the
*Examples* at the bottom can be copy-pasted. Python's equivalent is `help()` — e.g.
`help(len)`, or `help(np.arange)` once numpy is loaded — and the online documentation for
numpy and pandas is excellent. For anything the help pages cannot answer, the internet is
full of people who had your exact error message before you — Stack Overflow in particular.
Reading other people's answers is a core programming skill, not cheating.

## R as a glorified calculator

At its heart, the processor is a very fast calculator, and the console gives you direct
access to it. All the basic operations are here:

| Operation          | R             | Python        |
|--------------------|---------------|---------------|
| Add / subtract     | `2 + 3`, `2 - 3` | `2 + 3`, `2 - 3` |
| Multiply / divide  | `2 * 3`, `2 / 3` | `2 * 3`, `2 / 3` |
| Power              | `2^10`        | `2**10`       |
| Integer division   | `7 %/% 2`     | `7 // 2`      |
| Modulus (remainder)| `7 %% 2`      | `7 % 2`       |
| Square root        | `sqrt(2)`     | `math.sqrt(2)` |
| Natural log        | `log(2)`      | `math.log(2)` |
| Exponential        | `exp(1)`      | `math.exp(1)` |
| Trigonometry       | `sin(pi / 2)`, `cos(2 * pi)` | `math.sin(math.pi / 2)`, `math.cos(2 * math.pi)` |

: Basic mathematical operations in the two languages. `pi` is built into R; Python keeps it in the `math` library.

**Note for Python users:** the `math.` prefix in the right-hand column means those functions
live in the **math** *library*, which must be loaded — once, at the top of your script —
with `import math`. That includes the constant `math.pi`, since bare `pi` does not exist in
Python. Loading libraries is everyday Python life; numpy and pandas arrive later this
chapter in exactly the same way. And one trap deserves its own sentence: **the power
operator in Python is `**`**, because `^` exists there too but means something entirely
different (bitwise XOR) — `2^10` runs happily in Python and returns `8`. Ouch.

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
3 + 5 * 2
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
3 + 5 * 2
```

</div>
:::

In the R output, the `[1]` tells you that `13` is the first element of the answer — for now
answers have only one element, but that changes very soon (Python just prints the bare
number). Operations follow the usual algebraic precedence (powers, then multiplication and
division, then addition and subtraction, left to right), and parentheses override it:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
3 + 7 * 5 / 3 - 2
(3 + 7) * 5 / (3 - 2)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
3 + 7 * 5 / 3 - 2
(3 + 7) * 5 / (3 - 2)
```

</div>
:::

So any formula you can write on paper, you can type — for instance the one that circles
your lecturer's mind at 4am like a haunted seagull:
$$
\frac{\sqrt{3/4}}{\frac{1}{3} - \frac{2}{\pi^2}}.
$$
Here you go, be free, little bird:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
sqrt(3 / 4) / (1 / 3 - 2 / pi^2)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
import math   # sqrt, log, pi & co. live in the math library

math.sqrt(3 / 4) / (1 / 3 - 2 / math.pi**2)
```

</div>
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.1: A glorified calculator"}
Use the console to evaluate:

a.  $\dfrac{49^2 - 542}{42 + 63^2}$
b.  $\sqrt{\pi^3} - \cos(2\pi)$
c.  whether $2026$ is divisible by $7$, and whether it is divisible by $1013$
    (the `%%` operator — `%` in Python — is your friend: what should the remainder be?);
d.  each person's share when a £147.68 dinner bill is split among 7 people.
:::

## Variables and assignment

A calculator with no memory forces you to re-type intermediate results. Our languages
instead let you store any result in a **variable** — a labelled box in memory — using the
assignment operator: `<-` in R (read it as "gets"), the plain `=` in Python:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x <- 20 - 16
y <- 4 + 5
x - y
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x = 20 - 16
y = 4 + 5
x - y
```

</div>
:::

**Note on `<-` vs `=`:** R also accepts `=` for assignment, and Python users will type it
on reflex — but the R community's convention is `<-`, and we follow it in these notes.
Python offers no choice: assignment is `=`, and `<-` is not assignment at all there — in
Python `x <- 3` parses as "`x` less than `-3`", a comparison that quietly returns `True` or
`False`. Beware when switching columns.

Typing a variable's name prints its content, and the environment panel of RStudio lists
everything you have created:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x
y
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x
y
```

</div>
:::

Three things to know about assignment. First, both languages are case-sensitive, so `x` and
`X` are different names, and asking for a variable that does not exist is an error:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
#| error: true
X
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
#| error: true
X
```

</div>
:::

Second, assigning to an existing variable silently overwrites it — neither language asks
"are you sure?":

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x <- -100
x
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x = -100
x
```

</div>
:::

Third, a variable can appear on both sides of the assignment. The statement below is
nonsense as an equation but perfectly sensible as an instruction: *take the current value
of `x`, add 1, store the result back in `x`*:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x <- x + 1
x
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x = x + 1
x
```

</div>
:::

This little idiom is the beating heart of every iterative algorithm we will write in this
module, so stare at it until it feels normal.

Variables also make code readable. Compare the seagull formula from earlier with:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
numerator   <- sqrt(3 / 4)
denominator <- 1 / 3 - 2 / pi^2
numerator / denominator
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
numerator   = math.sqrt(3 / 4)
denominator = 1 / 3 - 2 / math.pi**2
numerator / denominator
```

</div>
:::

Same result, but each piece now has a name, can be inspected separately, and can be reused.
Name your variables like this — lowercase, words separated by `_`, meaning over brevity
(a convention both language communities happen to agree on).

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.2: Compound interest, minimal effort"}
You deposit £2000 in an account paying 3.5% interest per year. After $t$ years the balance
is $2000 \times 1.035^{t}$.

a.  Create variables `deposit`, `rate` and `years` (10 years), and compute the final
    balance *using only the variables*, storing it in `balance`.
b.  How much interest did you earn in total?
c.  A rival bank offers 5%. Change `rate`, re-run your lines, and report the new balance.
    Notice how little typing part (c) took: that is why we use variables.
:::

### Types, briefly

Not everything in a variable is a number. Both languages distinguish several **types** of
value, and R's `class()` — Python's `type()` — tells you which one you are holding:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
class(3.14)          # numeric: real numbers
class("statistics")  # character: text, always in quotes
class(TRUE)          # logical: TRUE or FALSE
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
type(3.14)          # float: real numbers
type("statistics")  # str: text, always in quotes
type(True)          # bool: True or False
```

</div>
:::

Numbers you know. **Character** values (strings) are text wrapped in quotes — without the
quotes, `statistics` would be the name of a variable. **Logical** values are the atoms of
decision-making in a program; @sec-week2 is largely about them, so we park them here.

**Note for Python users:** the type names differ — `float` for numeric, `str` for
character, `bool` for logical — and so does the spelling of the logicals: R shouts `TRUE`
and `FALSE` in full capitals, Python writes `True` and `False` with a capital initial only.
Each language rejects the other's spelling.

## Vectors {#sec-week1-vectors}

Statistics is not done one number at a time: you have $n$ observations, and you want to act
on all of them at once. R's fundamental data structure, the **vector**, is exactly that — an
ordered collection of values of the same type. The workhorse for creating one is `c()`,
short for *combine*.

**Note for Python users:** plain Python has *lists* — `[1.62, 1.85]`, square brackets —
but the object that matches R's vector, elementwise mathematics included, is the **array**
from the **numpy** library, the foundation of all scientific Python. Load it once per
script with `import numpy as np`; everything in it is then available as `np.something`, and
`np.array([...])` is your `c()`. Every vector and matrix in these notes goes through numpy.

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
heights <- c(1.62, 1.85, 1.71, 1.68, 1.79)   # heights in metres
heights
length(heights)   # how many elements?
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
import numpy as np                                    # load numpy once per script

heights = np.array([1.62, 1.85, 1.71, 1.68, 1.79])    # heights in metres
heights
len(heights)   # how many elements?
```

</div>
:::

Vectors of text work the same way (`c("Ada", "Bea", "Cal")`), but one vector cannot mix
types: if you try `c(1, "two")`, R silently converts everything to character — worth knowing
before it surprises you. (numpy plays it exactly the same: `np.array([1, "two"])` comes
back as two strings.)

### Sequences and repetitions

Typing long vectors by hand does not scale, so both languages give you generators. In R the
colon operator builds integer sequences, `seq()` builds general ones, and `rep()` repeats;
numpy's counterparts are `np.arange`, `np.linspace`, `np.tile` and `np.repeat`:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
1:10                                # integers from 1 to 10
5:-5                                # sequences can go downhill
seq(from = 0, to = 1, by = 0.1)     # step size 0.1
seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 5)  # exactly 5 equally spaced points
rep(c(1, 2), times = 3)             # repeat the whole vector 3 times
rep(c(1, 2), each = 3)              # repeat each element 3 times
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
np.arange(1, 11)                    # integers from 1 to 10 (end point EXCLUDED)
np.arange(5, -6, -1)                # sequences can go downhill
np.arange(0, 1.1, 0.1)              # step size 0.1 (stop just past 1 so 1 makes it in)
np.linspace(0, 1, 5)                # exactly 5 equally spaced points
np.tile([1, 2], 3)                  # repeat the whole vector 3 times
np.repeat([1, 2], 3)                # repeat each element 3 times
```

</div>
:::

**Note for Python users:** `np.arange(a, b)` stops *one step before* `b` — the end point is
excluded, which is why the integers 1 to 10 take `np.arange(1, 11)`. This end-exclusion
habit runs right through Python (it returns in slicing, below), so burn it in now.

`seq()` is our first function with named arguments: `from`, `to`, `by`, `length.out`.
Naming the arguments (rather than relying on their order) keeps calls readable — check
`?seq` for the full story. Python has named (*keyword*) arguments too:
`np.linspace(start = 0, stop = 1, num = 5)` reads just as well.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.3: Sequence like you mean it"}
Produce each of the following vectors in a single command, without typing out all the
elements:

a.  $0, 0.25, 0.5, \ldots, 3$
b.  $10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0$
c.  $1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3$
d.  $1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3$
e.  21 equally spaced points from $-1$ to $1$.
:::

### Vectorised arithmetic

Here is the superpower: arithmetic on vectors happens **elementwise**, with no extra effort
on your part. A scalar is applied to every element:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 77, 2, -2, 14)
x + 2
x * 10
x^2
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x = np.array([1, 2, 77, 2, -2, 14])
x + 2
x * 10
x**2
```

</div>
:::

Two vectors of the same length are combined element by element:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
y <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)
x + y
x * y
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
y = np.array([1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3])
x + y
x * y
```

</div>
:::

And mathematical functions map over every element too:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
sqrt(c(1, 4, 9, 16))
exp(c(0, 1, 2))
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
np.sqrt(np.array([1, 4, 9, 16]))
np.exp(np.array([0, 1, 2]))
```

</div>
:::

This style — one expression acting on $n$ numbers at once — is called **vectorised** code.
It is how R — and numpy, which exists for precisely this — wants to be written: compact,
close to the mathematical notation, and (as we will measure in @sec-week2) much faster than
handling elements one at a time.

Some functions instead *summarise* a whole vector into one number, which covers a good
share of day-one statistics:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
sum(heights)
mean(heights)
max(heights)
min(heights)
which.max(heights)   # the POSITION of the largest element
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
np.sum(heights)
np.mean(heights)
np.max(heights)
np.min(heights)
np.argmax(heights)   # the INDEX of the largest element -- counted from 0!
```

</div>
:::

(numpy also offers these as *methods* attached to the array itself — `heights.mean()` — a
spelling you will meet everywhere in the wild; the function form keeps our columns aligned.
And yes, `which.max` and `np.argmax` just disagreed by one about the same element — the
next-but-one section explains why.)

### Recycling, and its footgun

What if the two vectors have different lengths? R does not give up: it **recycles** the
shorter vector, repeating it until it matches the longer one. Sometimes that is exactly
what you want:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
1:6 + c(0, 100)     # c(0, 100) becomes 0, 100, 0, 100, 0, 100
1:6 * c(1, -1)      # alternating signs, in one command
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
np.arange(1, 7) + np.tile([0, 100], 3)   # numpy will NOT stretch a length-2 array: tile it yourself
np.arange(1, 7) * np.tile([1, -1], 3)    # alternating signs, repetition made explicit
```

</div>
:::

**Note for Python users — recycling vs broadcasting:** numpy does *not* recycle. Its rule,
called **broadcasting**, only stretches a scalar (or, once we reach matrices, a length-1
axis) to fit; two vectors of lengths 6 and 2 simply refuse to combine, with an error, not a
warning. That is why the Python column above repeats the short array explicitly with
`np.tile`. You lose a convenience and dodge a footgun — many would call that a win.

R only complains when the longer length is not a multiple of the shorter — and even then
it is a *warning*, not an error, and you still get an answer. numpy, meanwhile, refuses
outright and names the two shapes it could not reconcile:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
1:6 + c(0, 10, 100, 1000)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
#| error: true
np.arange(1, 7) + np.array([0, 10, 100, 1000])
```

</div>
:::

This is the footgun: if your two vectors were *supposed* to be the same length and are not
— say a typo dropped an observation — R may silently recycle and hand you plausible-looking
garbage. When a warning like the one above appears, treat it as an error until proven
innocent, and check your `length()`s. (**Note for Python users:** this footgun is R-only —
numpy's refusal to broadcast mismatched lengths turns the silent bug into an immediate,
honest error.)

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.4: The recycling plant"}
For each command, write down your predicted output *before* running it, then check.
One point per correct prediction, minus ten if you skip the predicting part.

a.  `1:6 + c(0, 10)`
b.  `c(1, 2, 3) * c(1, -1)`
c.  `1:8 / c(1, 2, 4, 8)`
d.  `(1:3)^(1:6)`

*Python users:* translate each expression into numpy (`np.arange`, `np.array`) and predict
instead whether numpy *runs it or raises an error* — and, for those that refuse, reproduce
R's answer with an explicit `np.tile`.
:::

### Indexing: getting elements out

Every element of a vector has a position — and here the two languages part ways in the most
consequential fashion of the whole module: R counts positions from 1, like humans and
mathematicians; Python counts from 0. Square brackets extract elements by position:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x <- c(5, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7)
x[1]           # first element
x[3]           # third element
x[length(x)]   # last element, whatever the length is
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x = np.array([5, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7])
x[0]           # first element
x[2]           # third element
x[len(x) - 1]  # last element (see the note: x[-1] is slicker)
```

</div>
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="1-based vs 0-based indexing (read this twice)"}
R counts positions **from 1**, Python **from 0**: the first element is `x[1]` in R but
`x[0]` in Python, and the element in position $k$ of your maths is `x[k]` in R but
`x[k - 1]` in Python.

Negative indices are worse than different — they are *false friends*. In R, `x[-1]` means
"everything **except** the first element". In Python, `x[-1]` means "count **from the
end**": it *is* the last element (a beloved idiom — no `len(x) - 1` needed). The same
characters, two entirely different results, and no error message to warn you. More
translation bugs are born on this line than anywhere else: when in doubt, print and check.
:::

The index can itself be a vector, which lets you take slices, cherry-pick, or reorder:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x[2:4]         # elements 2 to 4
x[c(1, 5)]     # elements 1 and 5
x[c(5, 1)]     # same elements, opposite order
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x[1:4]         # elements 2 to 4: indices 1, 2, 3 -- the slice EXCLUDES its end
x[[0, 4]]      # elements 1 and 5
x[[4, 0]]      # same elements, opposite order
```

</div>
:::

(There is the end-exclusion again: Python's slice `a:b` runs from index `a` up to, but not
including, index `b` — just like `np.arange`.)

A **negative** index means "everything except" in R — and something else entirely in
Python:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x[-1]          # drop the first element
x[-c(2, 3)]    # drop the second and third
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
np.delete(x, 0)        # drop the first element -- x[-1] would NOT do this...
np.delete(x, [1, 2])   # drop the second and third
x[-1]                  # ...because in Python this counts from the end
```

</div>
:::

And indexing on the left of the assignment overwrites elements in place:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x[3] <- 100    # replace the third element
x
x[c(1, 2)] <- 0  # replace several at once
x
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
x[2] = 100     # replace the third element
x
x[[0, 1]] = 0  # replace several at once
x
```

</div>
:::

One teaser before we move on: in both languages, brackets also accept conditions, so
`x[x > 50]` returns the elements larger than 50. How and why that works is the business of
@sec-week2 — resist the urge for one more week.

:::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.5: Marking spree"}
Ten students sat a test, scoring (out of 100):

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
#| eval: false
marks <- c(63, 58, 71, 45, 82, 69, 77, 52, 88, 60)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
#| eval: false
marks = np.array([63, 58, 71, 45, 82, 69, 77, 52, 88, 60])
```

</div>
:::

a.  Compute the mean mark and the range (maximum minus minimum).
b.  Which student (i.e. which *position*) got the top mark? Extract their mark using that
    position — in one command, without typing the position yourself.
c.  Extract the marks of students 2, 5 and 9 in a single command.
d.  Extract everyone *except* student 4, who has an exceptional-circumstances claim pending.
e.  The lecturer, feeling generous, adds 3 marks to everyone. Compute the new vector and
    its mean. How does the new mean relate to the old one, and why did that not require
    any statistics?
::::

### A first plot

Two vectors of equal length are begging to be plotted against each other, and base R
obliges with `plot()`; Python's counterpart is the **matplotlib** library:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
x <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.1)
y <- x^2 - x
plot(x, y, type = "l")   # type = "l" joins the points with a line
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt   # Python's plotting library

x = np.arange(-3, 3.1, 0.1)
y = x**2 - x
plt.plot(x, y)    # plt.plot draws a line by default
plt.show()
```

</div>
:::

That is genuinely all it takes to graph a function. (One asymmetry: base R plots points
unless you ask for a line with `type = "l"`; matplotlib's `plt.plot` draws a line unless
you ask otherwise — `plt.scatter` is its point-plotter.) We will keep using quick
one-liners like this as visual checks, and do plotting *properly* — labels, colours,
themes, publication quality — in @sec-week4.

## Saving your work: csv files and the working directory

Variables live in memory, and memory is wiped when your session closes. To keep results —
or to share them with anyone who is not inside your session — you write them to a file on
disk. The standard exchange format for data is the **csv** (comma-separated values) file, a
plain text table that every spreadsheet and statistics package can read:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
lancaster_rain <- c(12.5, 8.0, 0.0, 3.2, 21.7)   # mm of rain, Mon-Fri. The 0.0 is a typo, surely
write.csv(lancaster_rain, file = "week1_rain.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
import pandas as pd                              # Python's table library

lancaster_rain = np.array([12.5, 8.0, 0.0, 3.2, 21.7])   # mm of rain, Mon-Fri. The 0.0 is a typo, surely
pd.DataFrame(lancaster_rain).to_csv("week1_rain_py.csv", index=False)
```

</div>
:::

**Note for Python users:** csv duty falls to **pandas**, Python's data-frame library
(imported as `pd` by near-universal convention). pandas thinks in tables, so the array is
wrapped in a `DataFrame` on its way to disk, and `index=False` is the counterpart of R's
`row.names = FALSE`. The Python column writes to `week1_rain_py.csv` — a different file
name from the R column, so the two languages never overwrite each other's work.

But *where* did that file go? Into your **working directory**: the folder on disk where
your session currently "stands". Any file name without a folder in front of it is read
from, or written to, this directory.

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
#| eval: false
getwd()          # print the current working directory
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
#| eval: false
import os
os.getcwd()      # print the current working directory
```

</div>
:::

You can point elsewhere with a **path**: `"data/week1_rain.csv"` means "inside the folder
`data` under the working directory", and `"../week1_rain.csv"` means "one folder up".

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
#| eval: false
write.csv(lancaster_rain, file = "data/week1_rain.csv")  # needs a 'data' folder to exist
write.csv(lancaster_rain, file = "../week1_rain.csv")    # parent directory
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
#| eval: false
pd.DataFrame(lancaster_rain).to_csv("data/week1_rain_py.csv")  # needs a 'data' folder to exist
pd.DataFrame(lancaster_rain).to_csv("../week1_rain_py.csv")    # parent directory
```

</div>
:::

Rather than hard-coding long paths like `"C:/Users/you/Desktop/stuff/..."` (which break the
moment the script moves to another machine), the sane workflow is to keep your scripts and
data in one folder and make that the working directory — in RStudio: *Session > Set Working
Directory > To Source File Location*.

Reading the file back in is the mirror image:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
rain_from_file <- read.csv("week1_rain.csv")
rain_from_file
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
rain_from_file = pd.read_csv("week1_rain_py.csv")
rain_from_file
```

</div>
:::

The printout looks slightly different from a vector: it has a column name (`x` in R;
pandas defaults to `0`) and numbered rows (from 0 in Python, naturally). That is because
`read.csv()` — and equally pandas' `read_csv()` — returns a **data frame**: the
table-shaped cousin of the vector, and the single most important object in applied
statistics. It gets the star treatment in @sec-week4; for now, csv out and csv in is all
we need.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.6: There and back again (a csv's tale)"}
a.  Create a vector `temps` with the daily maximum temperatures
    $4.2, 6.8, 7.5, 3.1, 5.0, 8.4, 6.9$ (°C, a week in a Lancaster spring).
b.  Write it to a file called `week1_temps.csv` (Python users: `week1_temps_py.csv`, so
    the two languages stay out of each other's way), without row names (pandas: without
    the index).
c.  Find the file on disk and open it with a plain text editor (Notepad, TextEdit) —
    *not* Excel. Describe what you see: how are the values laid out?
d.  Read the file back into a new variable and check the values survived the round trip.
e.  What does the file look like if you forget `row.names = FALSE` (`index=False`) in
    part (b)?
:::

## Matrices and a taste of linear algebra {#sec-week1-matrices}

You know matrices from linear algebra; both our languages know them too, and — R being
built by statisticians, numpy by numerical scientists — they are very good at them. A
matrix in R is a vector wrapped onto rows and columns by `matrix()`; in numpy, a matrix is
simply a 2-D array:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
A <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), nrow = 2)
A
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
A = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]).reshape(2, 3, order="F")   # "F" = fill column by column, like R
A
```

</div>
:::

Note the order: R fills matrices **column by column** by default. If your data reads row by
row (as it usually does on paper), say so with `byrow = TRUE`:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
A <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
A
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])   # a list of rows: numpy's natural reading order
A
```

</div>
:::

**Note for Python users:** numpy's own filling order is the opposite of R's — row by row
("C order"); the `order="F"` above ("Fortran order", the column-major convention R
inherited) was only there to imitate R's default. The idiomatic numpy build is the second
chunk's: hand `np.array` a list of rows and no reshaping is needed — the code looks like
the matrix.

The dimensions are always rows first, columns second:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
dim(A)     # rows, columns
nrow(A)
ncol(A)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
A.shape      # (rows, columns)
A.shape[0]   # rows
A.shape[1]   # columns
```

</div>
:::

You can also build matrices by gluing vectors together: `cbind()` (numpy:
`np.column_stack`) binds them as columns, `rbind()` (`np.vstack`) as rows — remember the
column one, it earns its keep in the challenge at the end of this chapter.

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
cbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))   # two columns
rbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))   # two rows
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
np.column_stack([[1, 2], [3, 4]])   # two columns
np.vstack([[1, 2], [3, 4]])         # two rows
```

</div>
:::

### Indexing a matrix

Same square brackets as vectors, now with two positions: `[row, column]`. Leaving one slot
empty (R) or putting a bare colon `:` in it (Python) means "all of them":

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
A[1, 2]    # row 1, column 2
A[2, ]     # all of row 2
A[, 3]     # all of column 3
A[, c(1, 3)]  # columns 1 and 3
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
A[0, 1]    # row 1, column 2 (0-based, as ever)
A[1, :]    # all of row 2
A[:, 2]    # all of column 3
A[:, [0, 2]]  # columns 1 and 3
```

</div>
:::

And `t()` — in numpy the `.T` attribute — transposes:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
t(A)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
A.T
```

</div>
:::

### Matrix arithmetic: `*` is not what you think

Here is the classic trap — and it is the same trap in both languages. The ordinary
arithmetic operators work on matrices exactly as they do on vectors — **elementwise**:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
B <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
C <- matrix(c(10, 20, 30, 40), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
B + C
B * C     # elementwise! NOT the matrix product
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
B = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
C = np.array([[10, 20], [30, 40]])
B + C
B * C     # elementwise! NOT the matrix product
```

</div>
:::

The actual matrix product — rows times columns, as in $\left(BC\right)_{ij} = \sum_k B_{ik}
C_{kj}$ — has its own operator: `%*%` in R, `@` in Python:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
B %*% C
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
B @ C
```

</div>
:::

The usual conformity rule applies: an $(n \times k)$ matrix can only `%*%` a
$(k \times m)$ one. Writing `*` where you meant `%*%` (or `@`) is a rite of passage in
either language; the resulting bug is nasty precisely because both versions run without
error and return a matrix of the same size. Check a small case by hand when in doubt —
which is, conveniently, the next exercise.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.7: Matrix products, by hand and by machine"}
Let
$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

a.  Compute $AB$ with pen and paper.
b.  Build `A` and `B` (mind R's filling order!) and verify your answer with `%*%`
    (Python: `@`).
c.  Compute `A * B` and explain, in one sentence, what your language did instead.
d.  Compute $B^\top\!A$ using `t()` and `%*%` (`.T` and `@`). Is it equal to $(AB)^\top$?
    Should it be?
:::

### Inverses, determinants and linear systems

The function with the most misleading name in base R, `solve()`, computes matrix inverses:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
B_inv <- solve(B)   # the inverse of B
B_inv
round(B %*% B_inv, 10)   # B times its inverse: the identity (up to rounding)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
B_inv = np.linalg.inv(B)   # the inverse of B
B_inv
np.round(B @ B_inv, 10)    # B times its inverse: the identity (up to rounding)
```

</div>
:::

**Note for Python users:** numpy files all of linear algebra under `np.linalg`, and names
things honestly: `np.linalg.inv` inverts, `np.linalg.solve` (coming below) solves systems,
`np.linalg.det` takes determinants. R's `solve()` carries the misleading-name burden alone.

(The `round()` is there because floating-point arithmetic leaves microscopic dust like
`2.2e-16` where exact zeros should be — more on that in @sec-week2.) The identity matrix
itself, should you need one, is `diag(2)` in R, `np.eye(2)` in Python.

A matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero, and `det()`
(`np.linalg.det`) will tell you:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
det(B)
S <- matrix(c(1, 2, 2, 4), nrow = 2)   # second column = 2 * first: singular
det(S)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
np.linalg.det(B)                 # -2, plus a speck of that floating-point dust
S = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])   # second column = 2 * first: singular
np.linalg.det(S)
```

</div>
:::

Asking for the inverse of a singular matrix fails loudly in both languages (an *error*,
not a warning — priorities in the right place):

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
#| error: true
solve(S)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
#| error: true
np.linalg.inv(S)
```

</div>
:::

The name `solve()` starts making sense with its two-argument form, which solves the linear
system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. For
$$
\begin{aligned}
x + 2y &= 5 \\
3x + 4y &= 6
\end{aligned}
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}}_{A}
\mathbf{x}
=
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}},
$$

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
A <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(5, 6)
solve(A, b)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
b = np.array([5, 6])
np.linalg.solve(A, b)
```

</div>
:::

Mathematically this is $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, and `solve(A) %*% b` (Python:
`np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`) gives the same answer — but the two-argument `solve(A, b)` /
`np.linalg.solve(A, b)` never forms the inverse explicitly, which is both faster and
numerically more stable. Statistics is full of linear systems (you are about to meet the
most famous one in Challenge 1.1), so this one-liner will follow you for the rest of your
career.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.8: Three equations, three unknowns"}
Consider the system
$$
\begin{aligned}
2x + y - z &= 8 \\
-3x - y + 2z &= -11 \\
-2x + y + 2z &= -3.
\end{aligned}
$$

a.  Build the coefficient matrix `A` and the right-hand side `b`.
b.  Check that the system has a unique solution (which function tells you?).
c.  Solve it, and verify your solution by computing `A %*% x_sol` (`A @ x_sol`) and
    comparing with `b`.
:::

### An `eigen()` teaser

One more linear-algebra tool, offered now as a trailer. In statistics, the **covariance
matrix** of a random vector packages the variances (diagonal) and covariances
(off-diagonal) of its components. Its eigendecomposition is remarkably informative:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
Sigma <- matrix(c(4, 2, 2, 3), nrow = 2)   # a 2x2 covariance matrix
eigen(Sigma)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
Sigma = np.array([[4, 2], [2, 3]])   # a 2x2 covariance matrix
evals, evecs = np.linalg.eig(Sigma)
evals
evecs
```

</div>
:::

**Note for Python users:** `np.linalg.eig` hands back a *pair* — eigenvalues, eigenvectors
— rather than R's single object, and unlike R it makes no promise about their order (here
it happens to match R's largest-first). For symmetric matrices — and covariance matrices
always are — the specialised `np.linalg.eigh` is faster, more accurate, and sorts
eigenvalues in *ascending* order, so the "top" eigenvalue comes last.

The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue points in the direction along which the data
varies most, and the eigenvalues split the total variance across those directions — this
single idea is principal component analysis, the workhorse of dimension reduction.
Eigenvalues will also quietly reappear in @sec-week5, where they govern how fast our
optimisation algorithms converge. For now: `eigen()` (and `np.linalg.eig`) exists, and
Challenge 1.2 lets you poke at it.

:::: {.callout-important title="Challenge 1.1: Least squares, a sneak preview"}
A company records advertising spend $x$ (in £1000s) and sales $y$ (also £1000s) over eight
campaigns:

::: {style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr)); grid-column-gap: 10px;"}
<div>

**R**

```{r}
#| eval: false
x <- c(1.0, 1.9, 3.1, 3.8, 5.2, 6.0, 7.1, 8.2)
y <- c(2.4, 3.9, 6.3, 7.4, 10.4, 11.7, 14.1, 16.3)
```

</div>

<div>

**Python**

```{python}
#| eval: false
x = np.array([1.0, 1.9, 3.1, 3.8, 5.2, 6.0, 7.1, 8.2])
y = np.array([2.4, 3.9, 6.3, 7.4, 10.4, 11.7, 14.1, 16.3])
```

</div>
:::

The best-fitting line $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ (in the least-squares sense) has
coefficients
$$
\boldsymbol{\hat\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y},
$$
where $X$ is the matrix whose first column is all 1s and whose second column is $x$.

a.  Build $X$ with `cbind()` (a neat trick: `cbind(1, x)` recycles the 1). In Python —
    no recycling there — build the column of ones explicitly:
    `np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])`.
b.  Compute $\boldsymbol{\hat\beta}$ with `t()`, `%*%` and `solve()` (Python: `.T`, `@`
    and `np.linalg.inv` — or better, `np.linalg.solve`).
c.  Plot the data with `plot(x, y)` and overlay your line with
    `abline(a = beta[1], b = beta[2])`. (matplotlib has no `abline`: use
    `plt.scatter(x, y)`, then draw the line yourself with
    `plt.plot(x, beta[0] + beta[1] * x)`.) Admire.

You have just fitted your first regression, with your bare hands, using only week-1
material. In @sec-week5 we will fit models like this by *optimisation* — and see exactly
where this magic formula comes from.
::::

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge 1.2: Dissecting a covariance matrix"}
Take the $3 \times 3$ covariance matrix
$$
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}
2.0 & 0.8 & 0.4 \\
0.8 & 1.5 & 0.6 \\
0.4 & 0.6 & 1.0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

`eigen(Sigma)` returns an object with two pieces, which you can extract as
`eigen(Sigma)$values` and `eigen(Sigma)$vectors` (more on the `$` in @sec-week4). In
Python the two pieces arrive directly as a pair:
`evals, evecs = np.linalg.eig(Sigma)`.

a.  Verify numerically that the eigenvalues sum to the *total variance*
    $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)$, the sum of the diagonal (see `?diag`; Python: `np.diag`,
    or `np.trace` for the whole job).
b.  Store the eigenvector matrix as `V` and compute `t(V) %*% V` (`V.T @ V`), rounded to
    10 decimal places. What matrix do you get, and what does that say about the
    directions the eigenvectors describe?
c.  What proportion of the total variance lies along the first eigenvector? In
    principal-component speak, that is the "variance explained by PC1".
:::

## What you can do now

-   Use R or Python as a calculator, keep results in variables, and organise it all in
    commented scripts.
-   Build vectors with `c()`, `seq()` and `rep()` (numpy: `np.array`,
    `np.arange`/`np.linspace`, `np.tile`/`np.repeat`), slice them by position — minding
    who counts from 1 and who from 0 — and act on all elements at once with vectorised
    arithmetic; recycling (R) and broadcasting (numpy) warning bells installed.
-   Round-trip your data to disk as csv files (`write.csv`/`read.csv`; pandas'
    `to_csv`/`read_csv`), and know where your session put them.
-   Do real linear algebra: `%*%` (`@`), `t()` (`.T`), `det()`, `solve()` for inverses and
    systems (`np.linalg`'s `det`, `inv` and `solve`), and a first taste of `eigen()`
    (`np.linalg.eig`).

Next week, in @sec-week2, we teach the machine to make decisions: `TRUE` and `FALSE`
(`True` and `False`) in earnest, `if` and `else`, loops — and with them our first proper
algorithm, gradient descent, which will carry us all the way to @sec-week5.
